title: Beyond Accuracy: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Hypothesis-Driven Experiment Planning in LLM Agents
claim: A benchmark couples an agent-environment experimental loop with a diagnostic suite that scores outcomes, behavior and reasoning steps, not just final accuracy.
layout: 3 columns left-to-right: agent, environment, diagnostics; feedback arrows, bottom reasoning-trace loop
description: A wide three-part diagram with rounded boxes under colored pill titles. On the left, a purple 'Agent' box lists tasks (known candidate definitions, proposing initial concentrations) and shows a cartoon octopus holding test tubes. In the middle, a pink 'Environment' box shows test tubes, a padlock labeled 'Hidden mechanism (ground truth)', 'Simulate' and 'Fit candidates' steps, and a schematic concentration-vs-time plot with crossing substrate and product curves. Arrows labeled 'Propose' (right) and 'NLL feedback' (left) link agent and environment. On the right, orange 'Behavior' and 'Reasoning' boxes list diagnostics: identification accuracy, mechanism entropy, exploration mini-plots, and four numbered reasoning steps scored by LLM judges. An 'Experiment record' arrow and a bottom 'Reasoning trace' path feed the diagnostics. The eye goes first to the octopus and the colored headers.
caption: Overview of the benchmark and diagnostic evaluation framework. Agents distinguish among 20 candidate mechanisms over five experimental rounds on 200 reaction systems. In the agent--environment loop (left), the agent proposes an experimental condition $\alpha_k$. The environment simulates noisy kinetic time-series observations under a hidden ground-truth mechanism and returns negative log-likelihood (NLL) values obtained by fitting candidate mechanisms to the accumulated observations. The diagnostic framework (right) evaluates mechanism identification accuracy, mechanism entropy, and exploration behavior, and scores four reasoning steps of the agent's reasoning trace using LLM judges. The time-series curves, observation markers, and behavioral mini-plots are schematic.
abstract: Evaluating large language model (LLM) agents on scientific tasks typically reduces to final-task accuracy, which obscures where reasoning succeeds or breaks down. We introduce a benchmark and diagnostic evaluation framework for hypothesis-driven adaptive experimental planning in closed-world system identification, instantiated in kinetic mechanism identification. The framework goes beyond final accuracy in two ways. First, we evaluate exploration behavior by quantifying the extent to which agents exhibit space-filling or corner-seeking patterns in the experimental design space. Second, we decompose the reasoning process into four interpretable steps: belief update, hypothesis discrimination, discriminative experiment design, and predictive reasoning under interventions, each scored separately on reasoning traces. Across ten LLM agents, we find that stronger agents outperform both adaptive (Bayesian optimization) and non-adaptive (Latin hypercube) baselines and exhibit exploration patterns inconsistent with naive heuristics. Decomposing reasoning reveals that the stronger agents score consistently well across all four steps, whereas weaker agents often succeed at belief update and hypothesis discrimination but are less reliable at translating them into actionable designs and sharp contrastive predictions. Independent expert annotations support predictive reasoning under our stated validation criteria, while evidence for discriminative experiment design is positive but less consistent. The results suggest a gap between recognizing plausible hypotheses and translating them into contrastive predictions, with more tentative evidence for a corresponding experiment-design bottleneck. The benchmark website is available at https://schwallergroup.github.io/beyond-accuracy/.
